title: Cohort Audit: Anchoring Effects and NDCG Robustness Brief (Apr 2026)
summary: Short summary: This brief documents an audit of pairwise preference labeling and NDCG computations for the recent onboarding run (candidate model: opt-m-ond-2026-03). The audit focused on potential anchoring bias introduced by prompt templates, the effect of different tie-handling rules on NDCG, and stability of slice-level metrics across sampling cohorts. Primary outcome: global NDCG differences are small (<0.7% absolute) but several slices show systematic regressions (up to 3.2% NDCG drop) likely driven by prompt anchoring and long-response truncation. Recommended immediate actions: update prompt variants, expand pairwise adjudication for affected slices, and add bootstrap-based CI in the automated report pipeline.
sample_stats:
Sampling overview:
- Universe: logged rerank requests from hosted API (Jan-Mar 2026), filtered to 'search-like' routes and excluding bots.
- Pool size after filters: 1,120,452 requests.
- Candidate set size per request: variable (2-10), median=5.
- Drawn evaluation sample: 6,200 queries stratified by route and traffic-weighted frequency, with oversampling of long-tail routes (x2).
- Pairwise labeling plan: for each query, we generated all pairwise comparisons for top-5 candidates, randomly subsampled 8 pairs/query to limit annotation cost. Expected label count ~49,600.
- Actual collected labels: 48,732 (3.9% drop due to annotator timeouts).
- Annotator pool: 34 raters across two vendors (internal QA + vendor B).
- IAA (Kripp alpha) on a 1,200 overlap subset: 0.62 (moderate).
prompt_sets:
Prompt design and variants used in this audit:
- Baseline template (P0): short instruction + 3 anonymized candidate snippets + ask for preference. Example: "Which response best answers the user? Choose A or B."
- Long-context template (P1): includes additional 1-2 lines of context preceding the candidates (used to test anchoring).
- Default-system-instruction template (P2): includes a lead-in system note like "You are an expert assistant" (intended to increase formality).
- Perturbations: candidate order randomization was applied, but we discovered an implementation bug in 7% of tasks where the first candidate was shown in a bold font (visual anchor).
- Prompt-variant allocation: balanced across sample but vendors received slightly different distributions (vendor B saw P1 42% of the time vs 33% overall).
Notes: the visual-bias bug likely explains some first-item preferences in early batches. We recommend a rerun of 2k pairs with corrected UI to quantify the impact.
annotation_instructions:
Annotator instructions (condensed):
- Task: for each pair, select which response is better at answering the user intent. If equal quality, select 'no preference'.
- Preference criteria (priority order): correctness > relevance > helpfulness > conciseness > harmlessness.
- Edge-cases: when one response hallucinates factual details that change answer, prefer the non-hallucinating response even if shorter.
- Tie handling: encourage 'no preference' when differences are minor; aim for consistency with provided examples.
- QA checks: periodic gold insertion (5% of tasks) and mandatory adjudicator tie-break for disagreements flagged by IAA rules.
- Compensation and throughput: target 180 judgments/day per annotator, average time/pair=28s.
Annotation caveats: vendor-specific UI differences (see prompt_sets) and a non-negligible 'no preference' rate (11.6%) that affects DCG discounts.
ndcg_and_metrics:
NDCG calculation details and choices made in the audit:
- Relevance mapping: pairwise labels converted to relevance scores for each candidate via tournament aggregation: wins -> score 1, losses -> 0, no_preference -> 0.5.
- DCG formula used: DCG = sum_{i=1..k} (2^{rel_i} - 1) / log2(i+1).
- k (cutoffs) reported: NDCG@1, NDCG@3, NDCG@5.
- IDCG computed per-query based on ideal ordering from aggregated relevance.
- Tie-handling variations tested: (T0) no_preference=0.5 (baseline), (T1) treat no_preference as 0 (conservative), (T2) redistribute half-credit across tied items.
- Observations: T1 reduces NDCG uniformly by ~0.4-0.6 absolute points but amplifies apparent regressions on slices with high no-preference rates. T2 aligns closely with rank aggregation in tournament method but is more volatile for small candidate sets.
- Statistical significance: paired bootstrap (10k resamples) used to compute 95% CI on ΔNDCG between models. For global NDCG@5: Δ = -0.007 (95% CI [-0.012, -0.002]) between baseline and candidate model; p ≈ 0.003.
- Additional metrics collected: pairwise win-rate, percent-no-preference, mean-response-length, hallucination-flag rate (human), and Kendall-Tau between model predicted ranking and human ranking.
slice_definitions:
Slices used in slice-level analysis (descriptive):
- short-query: user prompt token length <= 6.
- long-query: user prompt token length >= 25.
- code-intent: queries labeled by heuristic as coding help (regex + route tag).
- citation-needed: queries that historically require external sources (route tag + keywords).
- long-candidate: at least one candidate length > 250 tokens (these are susceptible to truncation artifacts).
- high-ambiguity: pairwise gold overlap high (measured as pairwise no-preference rate > 20%).
- low-freq-route: routes in bottom 15% of traffic.
Notes: slices are not exclusive; overlap handled by per-slice independent aggregation and by a hierarchical debug view in the notebook.
analysis_results:
Key findings from slice-level analysis:
- Global: small but statistically significant NDCG@5 regression vs baseline (Δ=-0.007).
- long-candidate slice: largest negative impact, ΔNDCG@5 = -0.032 (95% CI [-0.044, -0.018]). Correlates with higher hallucination flags and response truncation.
- code-intent: slight positive lift ΔNDCG@3 = +0.009 (CI crosses zero), but effect sensitive to prompt variant P2.
- high-ambiguity: metrics noisy; percent-no-preference = 28% and NDCG estimates have wide CIs. For this slice, tie strategy dominates reported direction.
- short-query: negligible change but first-item bias was detected (first shown candidate chosen 13% more often than expected under randomization). This excess aligns with the visual-bias bug in the UI.
- vendor split: vendor B's subset shows larger ΔNDCG (more negative by ~0.012) driven by higher exposure to P1.
- Annotation quality signals: tasks with >2s median time had slightly higher agreement; low-time tasks concentrated in vendor B batch 2.
- Stability check: resampling cohorts (n=6k down to n=2k) shows variance increases rapidly under 2.5k queries; we recommend minimum 3k queries for reliable slice-level detection of ~1.5% effect sizes.
Tables and charts: detailed tables exported to the rerank-eval notebook (see linked_artifacts).
conclusions_and_actions:
Practical conclusions and recommended next steps:
1) Fix the UI visual-bias bug immediately and rerun a 2k-pair validation set to quantify first-item anchoring.
2) Prioritize prompt-variant standardization: reduce vendor divergence by enforcing P0/P2 parity.
3) For long-candidate slice: schedule a model truncation/regeneration check; consider candidate re-ranking with length-aware features or reranking model fine-tune.
4) Update automated reporting: include bootstrap 95% CI and a table showing sensitivity to tie-handling strategies (T0/T1/T2).
5) Expand adjudication for affected slices: add 3-way adjudication for 1,200 pairs sampled from long-candidate and high-ambiguity slices.
6) Add an explicit note in model onboarding checklist: minimum 3k stratified queries for slice-level regression detection and vendor UI parity confirmation.
Ownership: Aisha (analysis lead) + Jun (annotation ops) + Miguel (onboarding checklist update).
Timeline: immediate bug fix (1 week), validation rerun (2-3 weeks), onboarding checklist update (1 sprint).
notes_and_open_questions:
Open items and follow-ups:
- Quantify magnitude of visual-bias effect after UI fix: expected to reduce first-item over-selection by 8-12 percentage points.
- Should we change the canonical tie policy in the company NDCG playbook? Current evidence suggests T0 (0.5) is most stable across slices, but conservative teams prefer T1.
- Investigate whether vendor B's throughput incentives are correlated with lower median time and lower IAA — possible quality vs cost tradeoff.
- Consider adding a short automated prompt-variant audit that logs vendor/UI differences at collection time.
- Long-term: evaluate reranker candidate generation upstream (distance from oracle) to see if candidate set quality is the root cause for long-candidate regressions.
Quick links: audit notebook (github.com/redwood-inference/rerank-eval/tree/main/notebooks/cohort_audit.ipynb), PR with fix (see linked_artifacts).
